items.title: Azure AI Gateway Reaches General Availability as a Standalone Service
items.summary:

items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

items.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
items.summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

items.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
items.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy. AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. items.title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:announcing vllm gr efficient inference for generative recommendation
items.content_excerpt: Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. The overview shows how recommendation models generate item IDs or score supplied candidates. The OneRec-1.7B example below follows the generation path, from a viewer’s history to 128 candidate SIDs. A recommendation service has to turn a long interaction history into a set of candidates within a single request’s latency budget. Generating each item ID may take only a few tokens, yet the engine must explore many paths and return items the application can serve. vLLM-GR builds its recommendation search into the vLLM engine. vLLM supplies the scheduler, model execution, and paged KV cache. vLLM-GR adds a beam session that spans the whole search and keeps track of how candidate paths branch. EngineCore owns each beam session from admission to completion. The scheduler dispatches prefill and decode stages to a worker. At each stage, the model runner scores the next token and beam selection records the score and parent of each surviving path. The next decode uses those parent indices to read the right KV state. One request returns two candidates with beam widths of 2 → 3 → 2. The catalog filters out A1 · B1 because no item starts with that prefix. A full-vocabulary search skips this filter. The SIDs and scores are illustrative. In the prefill–decode–decode (PDD) pipeline, the scheduler admits a BeamSearch() request and dispatches its prefill stage to the worker. Prefill scores the first SID component while the host prepares decode 1. During decode 1, the host prepares decode 2. The second decode inherits the selected parents’ suffix KV and completes two SIDs. Green marks the component selected at each stage. The benchmarks measure P99 latency to show how beam width and batch size affect tail latency for generative recommendation. items.title: MeterRouter: Budget-Aware Dynamic Routing for Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) outperform single-agent systems, but inter-agent communication incurs substantial token overhead. While assigning a large LLM to every agent is common, it results in inefficient resource utilization, leaving the system far from the Pareto frontier. The cost of answering a query is set jointly by how many agents are recruited, the role and LLM assigned to each, and communication topology among them. Most existing routers treat cost only implicitly rather than as an explicit optimization constraint. A fixed accuracy-cost preference also cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a particular query. We introduce MeterRouter, a budget-aware dynamic router that incrementally synthesizes a collaboration graph by selecting each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and termination conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. We initialize the router by imitating successful execution graphs, then jointly refine its decisions with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, MeterRouter is (1) accurate, achieving performance comparable to the strongest MAS; (2) economical, reaching that accuracy at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router and extending the accuracy-cost frontier beyond the ceiling of single-agent systems; and (3) controllable, adapting its spending to the specified budget while rarely exceeding it.

items.title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
items.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.

items.title: Introducing Search for Agents
items.summary: Flip one toggle to make your site searchable by AI agents — complete with automatic content indexing, a discoverable search API, and native HTTP QUERY support.
items.content_excerpt: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall ( WAF ) configurations). Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site. items.title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
items.summary:
For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. 

Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway

To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud:

  • Workspace MCP servers: Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

  • Workspace CLI: Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor.

Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs.

Consistent controls across every agent workflow

Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today:

  1. Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools.

  2. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files.

  3. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure.

  4. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console, and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately.

  5. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices.

  6. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately.

Getting started

  • Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide, implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum.

  • Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console.

  • Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits.

With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).
